newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba holds symposium on once-banned Beatles.
newsitem.headline: Cuba holds symposium on once-banned Beatles.

text.p: The life and works of the Beatles, at one time banned in Cuba because they were viewed as contrary to revolutionary culture, were given a full airing on Tuesday at the start of a symposium on the group.

The three-day meeting in a Havana cultural centre, organised by Cuba's Union of Writers and Artists (UNEAC), will include papers on different aspects of the British band, films about the group and a concert Thursday by Cuban musicians.

Several dozen fans attended the meeting, some wearing Beatles T-shirts. The British Council, a British government cultural institute, presented the gathering with a photographic exhibition and a state television choir opened the event with renditions of Beatles songs.
"The fact they were banned here perhaps gave them a higher profile than elsewhere in Latin America," a British Embassy spokesman told Reuters.

The Beatles were banned in Cuba in the mid-1960s, just as they were reaching cult status around the world, because they were viewed by Fidel Castro's government as undesirable in a culture that sought to impose an ethic of work and sacrifice.
Although they were not American, the fact they sung in English did not help -- the early years after Castro's 1959 revolution were characterised by deep tensions with the United States.

Cuban authorities also wanted to prevent the arrival of the drugs and hippie culture on the island. At the time, the Education Ministry banned male students from having long hair and women students from wearing mini-skirts, prohibitions that have also long since disappeared. UNEAC president Abel Prieto now wears his hair in a trailing mane.

By the mid-1970s the Beatles were to be heard frequently on Cuban radio and in 1985 the Beatles film "A Hard Day's Night" was aired on Cuban state television. Since then Cuban television has shown numerous documentaries on the Liverpool group.

A Cuban expert on cultural affairs, Remmy Martinez, said the meeting this week, while it did not represent a sudden leap into tolerance since the Beatles had long been accepted, was part of efforts to "eliminate the legacy of prejudice".
Martinez added that the period from 1963 to about 1967 was very culturally closed in Cuba. "It was a moment of self-defence of the revolution," he said.
Despite the ban on the national airwaves, fans listened to the music in their homes or tuned into U.S. radios. There are Cubans of 40 to 50 years old who show remarkable knowledge of the group.
And, said one fan at the Havana meeting, the appeal is not just for a certain generation. "I know one 12-year-old girl who has collected all their records," he said.
